basics: Blood is a fluid that has to be moved round a closed loop of tubes by a pump. The loop is actually two loops joined in series: the right half of the heart pushes blood through the lungs (pulmonary circulation) so it can pick up oxygen and dump carbon dioxide, and the left half pushes that oxygen-rich blood through every other organ (systemic circulation). Vessels leaving the heart are arteries, vessels returning are veins, whatever gas the blood carries; that is why the pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood. The atria are the receiving chambers, the ventricles the pumping chambers. Because the two loops are in series, the volume pumped per minute by each side must be equal on average; the slide does not say that the systemic loop runs at roughly five times the pressure of the pulmonary loop.

basics: Before learning what the heart does, you need to know where it sits. Anatomists describe position relative to an upright body facing you: a vertical line down the middle of the breastbone (sternum) is the midsternal line. The heart is roughly the size of your fist and lies behind the sternum, resting on the diaphragm (the dome of muscle separating chest from abdomen), with about two thirds of its mass to the left of the midline. Its pointed tip, the apex, points down, forward and to the left, near the fifth rib space; its broad base is at the top and back. This is why chest compressions on the lower sternum squeeze the heart against the spine. The slide gives no measurements; the book gives approximate dimensions and mass.

basics: The chest cavity is not one open space. Each lung sits in its own bag (pleural cavity), and everything between the two lungs, from the breastbone in front to the spine behind and from the first rib down to the diaphragm, is called the mediastinum. Clinicians subdivide it: a horizontal plane through the sternal angle (the bump where the manubrium meets the sternal body, level with the second rib) separates the superior mediastinum above from the inferior mediastinum below; the inferior part is further split into anterior (in front of the pericardium), middle (the heart in its pericardium) and posterior (behind it: oesophagus, descending aorta). A mid-sagittal section is a cut in the vertical front-to-back plane through the midline. Tortora defines the mediastinum but does not subdivide it.

basics: Imagine pushing your fist into a partly inflated balloon: the rubber touching your fist is the visceral layer, the outer rubber is the parietal layer, and the thin space between them is the cavity. That is how every serous membrane works, and the pericardium is the one round the heart. It has two main parts: a tough outer bag of dense connective tissue, the fibrous pericardium, anchored to the diaphragm and the great vessels, and inside it a thin double-layered serous pericardium. The parietal serous layer is stuck to the inside of the fibrous bag; the visceral serous layer (also called the epicardium) is stuck to the heart. Between them a few millilitres of pericardial fluid let the beating heart slide without friction. The slide's sentence about the fibrous pericardium should be read this way: it fuses with the parietal layer, not directly with the heart surface.

basics: The mitral valve is the two-flap door between left atrium and left ventricle, named after a bishop's two-peaked hat. Valves in the heart have no muscle of their own; they are passive flaps of connective tissue covered by endocardium that swing according to which side has higher pressure. When the ventricle relaxes and atrial pressure is higher, the cusps hang open into the ventricle. When the ventricle contracts, the rising pressure pushes the cusps up until their edges meet; simultaneously the papillary muscles contract and tighten the chordae tendineae, so the cusps cannot flip into the atrium. Because the left ventricle generates the highest pressures, this valve suffers most from wear: it can narrow (stenosis) or leak (insufficiency, prolapse).

basics: Muscle thickness follows workload. Both ventricles eject the same volume per beat, but the right one pushes it only through the low-resistance lungs at roughly 25 mmHg, whereas the left must drive it round the whole body against about 120 mmHg. So the left ventricular wall is about three times thicker (10-15 mm versus 4-5 mm), its cavity is round in cross-section, and the thinner right ventricle wraps round it as a crescent. Atria, which only top up the ventricles, are thinnest of all. The muscle fibres are not simply circular: they run in spiral bundles that wrap the ventricles like a twisted towel, which is what the slide calls the myocardial vortex; when they shorten, the apex twists and the chamber is wrung out rather than squeezed.

basics: A pump needs valves so that squeezing pushes fluid forward rather than back. The heart's valves are passive: nothing pulls them open or shut except the pressure difference across them. When a ventricle fills, atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure and the AV valve hangs open; when the ventricle contracts, its pressure exceeds atrial pressure and the cusps are pushed together, with the chordae tendineae stopping them everting. Once ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure the semilunar valve is pushed open; when the ventricle relaxes, blood starting to fall back fills the cup-shaped cusps and slams them shut. That slamming, or rather the turbulence it causes, is the heart sound: AV closure gives the first sound, semilunar closure the second. Notice there are no valves where the veins enter the atria.

basics: An AV valve is like a parachute anchored by cords. basics: Before birth the placenta, not the lungs, oxygenates the blood, and the collapsed fluid-filled lungs offer very high resistance. basics: Muscle cells contract because arrays of actin and myosin filaments slide past each other, and in skeletal and cardiac muscle these arrays are lined up so the cell looks striped (striated). Cardiac cells differ from skeletal ones in being short, branched, usually one-nucleus, and joined end to end by intercalated discs. Each disc contains desmosomes, rivet-like junctions that stop the cells tearing apart when they pull, and gap junctions, tiny channels that let ions and hence the electrical signal pass directly from cell to cell. That coupling makes all the cells of the atria (and separately of the ventricles) fire and contract as a unit, a functional syncytium. Cardiac cells are packed with mitochondria (about a quarter of the cell volume) and never rest, and their contraction is not under conscious control.

basics: Every cell keeps a voltage across its membrane by pumping ions and letting some leak; most excitable cells sit at a stable negative resting potential and fire only when something pushes them to threshold. basics: Read the graph as a repeating loop. From its most negative point (about -60 mV) the SA cell's voltage ramps slowly upward because special channels open at negative voltages and let a small inward sodium leak in (the 'funny' current); the slope of this ramp is the timer. When the ramp reaches threshold, voltage-gated calcium channels open and calcium rushes in, giving the sharp upstroke (unlike nerve cells, which use sodium for the spike). Then calcium channels close and potassium channels open; potassium flows out and the voltage falls back to -60 mV, which re-arms the funny channels and the loop restarts. One loop per 0.8 s gives 75 beats per minute. Anything that steepens the ramp (sympathetic nerves, adrenaline) speeds the heart; anything that flattens it (vagus nerve, acetylcholine) slows it.

refs.capture: p.744 right column, heading 'Action Potential and Contraction of Contractile Fibers' and step 1 'Depolarization' (start 'Unlike autorhythmic fibers, contractile fibers'), continuing on p.746 left column with step 2 'Plateau' and step 3 'Repolarization'; p.746 right column, the two paragraphs starting 'The mechanism of contraction is similar' and 'In muscle, the refractory period' (why tetanus cannot occur); p.746 Figure 20.11 (top of page; the slide reproduces it)

basics: A working ventricular cell rests at about -90 mV and fires only when a neighbour's impulse arrives through gap junctions. Its action potential has three phases. Fast sodium channels open and sodium floods in: the voltage shoots to about +20 mV in a millisecond. Then, instead of falling straight back as in a nerve, the voltage sits near 0 mV for about 0.2 s: slow calcium channels are letting calcium in while some potassium is leaving, and the two currents balance (plateau). The entering calcium releases more calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and this calcium triggers the sliding of filaments, so contraction follows. Finally more potassium channels open, calcium channels close, and the cell repolarises. The whole event lasts about 0.3 s, during which the cell cannot be re-fired (refractory period), which is longer than the contraction itself, so the heart cannot go into sustained cramp (tetanus) and always relaxes to refill.

The prolonged phase of maintained depolarisation near 0 mV unique to cardiac muscle.
The cell's internal calcium store, which releases Ca2+ to trigger contraction.

basics: When millions of heart cells depolarise together, the moving front of charge creates a small electric field that reaches the skin; electrodes on limbs and chest record it as the ECG, a voltage-versus-time trace in millivolts. It is not a recording of contraction but of the electrical events that cause it. The P wave is atrial depolarisation; the QRS complex is ventricular depolarisation (large because the ventricles are massive), and it hides the simultaneous atrial repolarisation; the T wave is ventricular repolarisation. The gaps carry information too: the P-R (Tortora: P-Q) interval is the conduction time through the atria and the AV node delay; the flat S-T segment is the plateau when all ventricular cells are depolarised; the Q-T interval spans the whole ventricular electrical cycle. Heart rate is 60 divided by the R-R interval in seconds.

terms.d: A skin contact, and the voltage difference measured between a pair of contacts.
The small first bump: atria depolarising.
The sharp spike: ventricles depolarising.
The rounded bump after QRS: ventricles repolarising.
A time span that includes at least one wave (e.g. P-R, Q-T).
A flat time span between waves (e.g. S-T).
One thousandth of a volt; ECG deflections are about 1 mV.

basics: This slide lines up the ECG with the seven mechanical phases the lecturer labels A to G, a finer division than Tortora's three periods. The logic is simple: electrical events come first and mechanical events follow a fraction of a second later. Just after the P wave the atria contract (A). Just after the QRS the ventricles contract: first with all valves shut (B, isovolumetric contraction), then ejecting rapidly (C) and more slowly (D) as the T wave appears. After the T wave the ventricles relax with all valves shut (E, isovolumetric relaxation), then fill rapidly once the AV valves open (F), then slowly (G, diastasis) until the next P wave. Tortora lumps C and D as ventricular ejection and F and G as ventricular filling.

basics: A cardiac cycle is one complete heartbeat, from one P wave to the next. Because the atria and ventricles are excited in sequence, the cycle is atrial systole with ventricular diastole, then ventricular systole with atrial diastole, then a period when everything is relaxed. At 75 beats per minute one cycle takes 0.8 s: roughly 0.1 s atrial contraction, 0.3 s ventricular contraction, 0.4 s total relaxation. The same 0.8 s can be described in five parallel ways, which the slide lists and Tortora stacks in one figure: the ECG (electrical), which chambers are contracting (mechanical), the pressures in atrium, ventricle and aorta, the heart sounds, and the ventricular volume. The following slides take each row in turn; the key idea linking them is that pressure differences open and close the valves.

basics: Ventricular systole has two parts. First, isovolumetric contraction: the ventricles begin to squeeze, pressure inside jumps above atrial pressure so the AV valves slam shut (first heart sound), but pressure is still below that in the aorta and pulmonary trunk so the semilunar valves stay shut too. With all four valves closed the blood is trapped and, since liquids are almost incompressible, the volume cannot change while the pressure climbs steeply; the muscle is tensing without shortening. The slide's 'Boyle's law' reference is a loose analogy, since Boyle's law is for gases. Second, ejection: once ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure (about 80 mmHg on the left, 20 on the right) the semilunar valves open and blood is pushed out, ventricular volume falls by about 70 mL, and ventricular and aortic pressures rise together to the systolic peak of about 120 mmHg.

basics: Diastole is when the ventricles refill, and most of the cycle is spent in it (0.4 s of relaxation plus 0.1 s atrial systole out of 0.8 s). As the ventricles relax their pressure drops below arterial pressure; blood starts to fall back, catches in the semilunar cusps and closes them (second heart sound), with a small rebound bump on the aortic trace called the dicrotic wave. Briefly all four valves are shut again (isovolumetric relaxation): pressure falls fast, volume stays at the end-systolic level. When ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure the AV valves drop open and blood that has been piling up in the atria pours in: about three quarters of filling is this passive early rush. Then the atria contract and add the last quarter, so the ventricle reaches its end-diastolic volume (about 130 mL). Faster heart rates shorten diastole more than systole, so filling suffers first.

basics: A Wiggers diagram is the name physiologists give to the stacked plot of ECG, pressures, sounds and volume against time for one cycle; Tortora's Figure 20.14 is one. The organising rule is that valves are pure pressure switches. Follow the left ventricle: the atrium contracts and adds its 20-25% top-up; the ventricle contracts, its pressure passes atrial pressure and the mitral valve shuts (S1, point 5); pressure climbs with all valves shut; at about 80 mmHg it passes aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens (point 6); ejection continues to a peak of about 120 mmHg; the ventricle relaxes, pressure falls below aortic and the aortic valve shuts (S2, dicrotic notch, point 9); pressure keeps falling with all valves shut; below atrial pressure the mitral valve reopens (point 10) and filling begins. Note Tortora places aortic valve closure at about 100 mmHg.

basics: Smooth flow is silent; sound is made by turbulence. Each valve closure abruptly stops a column of moving blood and sets it vibrating, and those vibrations are the heart sounds. S1 ('lub') comes from AV valve closure at the start of ventricular systole; it is longer and louder. S2 ('dub') comes from semilunar closure at the start of diastole. A phonocardiogram is simply a microphone trace of these. Two further sounds exist but are normally too faint to hear: S3, from blood rushing into the ventricle during rapid filling, and S4, from atrial contraction pushing into the ventricle. The slide adds the clinical meaning: an audible S3 in an adult suggests an over-filled, floppy ventricle (volume overload, heart failure), an S4 suggests the atrium fighting a stiff ventricle (pressure overload). Tortora gives only the physical causes.

basics: A stethoscope hears vibrations conducted to the chest wall. The four valves lie close together behind the sternum, so if you listened directly over them the sounds would overlap. Instead the sound travels downstream with the blood, so each valve is best heard where its outflow comes nearest the surface: aortic valve at the right second intercostal space, pulmonary at the left second space, tricuspid at the lower left sternal border, mitral at the apex in the left fifth space. Listening this way an examiner checks rhythm, the timing and splitting of S1 and S2, extra sounds (S3, S4) and murmurs, which are whooshes produced by turbulent flow through a narrowed valve (stenosis) or a leaking one (incompetence). Timing tells which valve: a murmur between S1 and S2 is systolic.

basics: The volume trace is the easiest row to read because volume can only change when a valve is open. basics: Cardiac output is the flow rate delivered by one ventricle: volume per beat times beats per minute. Stroke volume is what leaves per beat, and it equals what was in the ventricle at the end of filling minus what is left after ejection. So at rest about 70 mL times about 75 beats gives about 5 L per minute, which is roughly the whole blood volume, meaning your entire blood supply passes through each side of the heart about once a minute. Both ventricles must have the same output on average or blood would pile up in one circuit. Output can rise four- to fivefold in exercise by raising both rate and stroke volume. The slide uses 72 beats per minute (5.04 L/min); Tortora uses 75 (5.25 L/min). Either is a typical resting figure.

basics: The SA node sets a default rhythm, but demand changes, so two control layers adjust output. The nervous layer is the cardiovascular centre in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem. It receives reports from higher brain areas, from movement sensors in muscles and joints, from chemoreceptors watching blood oxygen, CO2 and acidity, and from baroreceptors watching arterial stretch, and it replies through two sets of nerves: sympathetic cardiac accelerator nerves release noradrenaline, raising both rate and force; the parasympathetic vagus nerves release acetylcholine, slowing the SA node. At rest the vagal brake dominates. The hormonal layer: adrenaline and noradrenaline from the adrenal medulla mimic the sympathetic nerves. Stroke volume also responds mechanically: more venous return stretches the ventricle, and a more stretched muscle contracts harder (Frank-Starling), so output rises without any nerve.

basics: A blood vessel is a tube with a three-layered wall. Innermost is the tunica intima: a single sheet of flat endothelial cells (continuous with the heart's endocardium) on a basement membrane, bounded in arteries by a fenestrated internal elastic membrane. The middle tunica media is rings of smooth muscle and elastic fibres; it is the layer that varies most and that contracts or relaxes to narrow or widen the lumen. The outer tunica externa is collagen and elastic fibres with nerves and, in big vessels, tiny nutrient vessels (vasa vasorum). Arteries have a thick media because they take pulsatile high pressure; veins have a thin media, no elastic membranes, a thick externa, a wider lumen and, in the limbs, one-way valves. Capillaries are just endothelium and basement membrane, one cell thick, for exchange.

basics: The answer to the slide's question is that vessels are a branching tree in both directions: the aorta divides into a few large elastic arteries, these into many medium muscular (distributing) arteries, these into hundreds of millions of arterioles and billions of capillaries; on the way back capillaries merge into venules, then medium veins, then the two venae cavae. Each generation of branch is narrower but there are far more of them, so the total cross-sectional area grows toward the capillaries. The wall changes with the job: elastic arteries have a media dominated by elastic sheets to smooth the pulse; muscular arteries have up to 40 layers of smooth muscle to direct flow; veins have thin walls, a big lumen and often valves. Very large vessels need their own small nutrient vessels, the vasa vasorum, and nerves in the externa.

basics: Think of the circulation as a river system that splits into countless streams and then rejoins. Three curves describe it. Pressure: highest and pulsing in the aorta (about 120/80 mmHg), falling gently through arteries, dropping steeply across the arterioles because their narrow muscular lumens are the main site of resistance, and smoothing to a steady few mmHg in capillaries and veins, reaching zero at the right atrium. Total cross-sectional area: small in the aorta, enormous in the capillary bed because billions of tiny tubes run in parallel, small again in the venae cavae. Velocity: by conservation of flow (flow = area times velocity, and the flow through every level is the same cardiac output), blood is fast in the aorta, crawls at under a millimetre per second in capillaries, giving time for exchange, and speeds up again in the veins.

basics: Flow through any tube obeys the same rule as current through a resistor: flow equals pressure difference divided by resistance. The heart provides one pressure head for the whole systemic circuit (mean arterial pressure minus roughly zero at the right atrium), and the organs are plumbed in parallel, so each organ's share is set by its own resistance. Resistance depends on three things: vessel length (fixed in the short term), blood viscosity (set mainly by the red-cell fraction), and above all lumen radius, since resistance rises with the fourth power of narrowing: halving the diameter multiplies resistance sixteen-fold. Arterioles therefore act as taps. Sympathetic nerves set their general tone, while local chemicals from active tissue (CO2, H+, K+, adenosine, nitric oxide) dilate the arterioles of exactly the tissues that are working, a process called autoregulation.

basics: By the time blood reaches the veins almost all the heart's pressure has been spent: about 16 mmHg in venules versus 0 at the right atrium. When you stand, the column of blood in your leg veins weighs enough to nearly cancel that small push. Two extra pumps help, both relying on the one-way valves in limb veins. In the skeletal muscle pump, contracting calf and thigh muscles squeeze the deep veins between them; blood can only go toward the heart because the valve above (proximal) opens and the valve below (distal) closes. When the muscle relaxes the compressed segment refills from below: the proximal valve closes, the distal one opens. Each step milks blood upward. The respiratory pump does the same using breathing-driven pressure changes in the abdomen and chest. Standing still for a long time defeats the pump and blood pools.

basics: Blood pressure is held steady by a negative-feedback loop like a thermostat. The sensors are baroreceptors, stretch-sensitive nerve endings in the wall of the carotid sinus (in the neck, feeding the brain) and the aortic arch. They fire faster when pressure stretches them more. Their signals travel in cranial nerves IX and X to the cardiovascular centre in the medulla, which compares them with the set point and adjusts three effectors: sympathetic accelerator nerves to the heart (rate and force up), vagus nerves to the heart (rate down), and sympathetic vasomotor nerves to arterioles and veins (constriction up or down). Pressure falls when you stand: baroreceptors fire less, the centre cuts vagal braking and raises sympathetic drive, so cardiac output and resistance rise and pressure recovers within seconds. Chemoreceptors add a second input, raising pressure when oxygen is low or CO2 and acid are high.

basics: Nerves fix pressure within seconds; hormones act over minutes to days, mainly by changing blood volume and vessel diameter. Four matter. When the kidneys sense low pressure or volume they release renin, an enzyme that starts a chain ending in angiotensin II, a powerful arteriole constrictor that also makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone, which tells the kidneys to keep sodium and hence water: volume and pressure rise. Adrenaline and noradrenaline from the adrenal medulla raise heart rate and contractility and constrict skin and gut arterioles while dilating those in muscle. Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary constricts vessels and makes the kidney retain water. Working the other way, atrial natriuretic peptide, released when the atria are over-stretched, dilates vessels and makes the kidney dump salt and water, lowering pressure.

basics: This is a multi-organ feedback loop for defending blood volume. Trigger: dehydration, salt loss or bleeding lowers blood volume and pressure. Sensor: juxtaglomerular cells in the kidney feel the lower pressure and secrete renin into the blood. Cascade: renin is an enzyme that clips angiotensinogen, a protein the liver constantly makes, into angiotensin I; as blood passes through the lungs, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) on the capillary lining clips that into angiotensin II, the active hormone. Two responses restore pressure: angiotensin II constricts arterioles directly, raising resistance, and it makes the adrenal cortex secrete aldosterone, which acts on kidney tubules to reclaim sodium and with it water (while dumping potassium and hydrogen ions) so blood volume rises. A separate trigger, high blood potassium, also releases aldosterone. ACE inhibitors, common blood-pressure drugs, block the lung step.
